summary: A 1977 proposed official standard for the format of ARPA Network messages. It was replaced by RFC 733.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 724 proposes a shared format for ARPA Network message headers and addresses. It separates headers from message text while allowing people and programs to read and process the fields.

questions: what message format did rfc 724 propose
how are headers separated from message text
subtitle: A proposal to standardize the format of ARPA Network messages.

tldr.problem: ARPANET message systems used differing header conventions, especially for recipient fields, making messages harder for other systems to interpret.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines a common message-header syntax, address forms, and a framework that places header fields before message text.
tldr.outcome: RFC 724 was a proposed message format and was obsoleted by RFC 733.

facts.label: Message parts
facts.value: Headers followed by a blank line and optional body text

today: RFC 724 was a proposed standard for ARPA Network message format and was obsoleted by RFC 733.

sections.title: Why a Message Format Was Proposed
sections.content:
The memo describes ARPA Network messages as using FTP's MAIL and MLFL commands as an interim delivery method. RFC 561 had suggested basic header fields, and RFC 680 had defined additional fields, but different systems still used incompatible conventions.

The authors propose a revision to RFCs 561 and 680. They emphasize that the document defines a message format passed between hosts; it does not require particular message-system features or user interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Network mail systems had added header fields in different ways. This proposal tries to give those systems one shared format.

sections.title: Headers and Message Text
sections.content:
The proposed message consists of header fields followed by a blank line and then optional message text. Each field has a name, a colon, and a body. Long header fields can be folded onto multiple lines when the continuation line begins with whitespace; a parser unfolds them into a single logical line.

The proposal identifies required date and originator information and defines optional fields such as To, cc, bcc, Subject, and user-defined fields. It also describes address syntax for mailboxes, groups, and references to stored address lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Headers come first, followed by a blank line and then the message text. Header fields label information such as sender, recipients, and subject.

sections.title: Addressing People and Groups
sections.content:
The proposal allows an address to refer to a mailbox, a group of addresses, or a stored address list. A person can have multiple mailboxes, and a group may include other groups. The syntax can also carry non-Network addresses, such as a postal address, though the ARPANET system is expected to ignore such addresses.

The RFC states that it provides no authentication mechanism. It distinguishes a claimed valid network address from free text included for human convenience.
sections.plainLanguage: An address can name one mailbox, several mailboxes, a group, or a stored list. The format does not authenticate who sent a message.

references.text: Chiappa, N., "Standardizing Network Mail Headers", RFC 561.
Pogran, K., Crocker, D., and J. Vittal, "Message Transmission Protocol", RFC 680.
